A map pin, a heart, and a shield sit on the left. The map pin is highlighted. The screenshot does not show which sections these buttons open.
The feed shows a text message and an image that looks like a sticker. Player names, icons, and timestamps appear next to messages.
The feed shows an energy request card with the labels “Me” and “Member” and a “Claim 50” button. The screenshot does not establish who can claim those 50 units or under what conditions.
The bottom bar has a “Say something…” field, a sticker icon, and a send arrow. The icon to the left of the field has no label.
contracts: Opening and closing chat

Chat opens on the Café the first time. On subsequent visits, it returns to the last tab the player can access. The window’s close button hides chat. Closing a private tab removes the tab, and the conversation history is available when it is reopened.

Closing the active conversation switches chat to the Café. If the last tab is no longer accessible, reopening chat also takes the player to the Café. A click inside chat must not activate a game object underneath it.
Who can see messages

Members of a public channel can see its messages. Only the two participants in a private conversation receive its history and new messages. The server checks access when a player reads history or sends a message.

Each tab has its own messages and draft. A response for a previously selected tab must not replace the current feed. When channel access is revoked, the old feed is hidden and the player can no longer send to that channel.
Unread messages and online count
Assume the red dot means a new message arrived and the player has not seen it yet. It clears when the last unread message is in view. A player’s own messages do not trigger the dot.
For testing, assume the Café counts players once, even if they open the game on two devices. When offline, the count is marked as stale or unavailable. It refreshes after reconnecting.
Message order and scrolling
After syncing, the feed follows the order set by the server. Receiving the same event twice does not add a second copy of the message. The client displays server timestamps in the player’s time zone.

Scrolling up loads older messages without moving the message the player was reading. While the player is reading history, new messages leave the scroll position in place and offer a way to jump to the latest messages. At the bottom of the feed, new messages come into view automatically.
Sending text
The send arrow posts to the active tab. Empty and whitespace-only messages cannot be sent. The client and server use the same way to measure length and apply the same limit.

The server response indicates whether the message was accepted or rejected. A rejected message can be edited and sent again. When a response is lost, retrying uses the original operation so the other player does not get two copies.
Stickers

The sticker icon opens the sticker picker. The test cases assume that choosing a sticker sends it immediately to the active tab and leaves the text draft in place. Closing the picker without choosing sends nothing.
The server checks whether the sticker is available to the player. If its image fails to load, the feed keeps a placeholder and offers a retry.
Requesting and claiming energy

The test cases assume that players in the channel can see the card and the server checks claim eligibility for each player. An eligible player gets 50 energy from a card once. Whether the player who posted the request can claim from it still needs confirmation.

The button shows a pending state while the server responds. A successful claim, an already claimed card, an expired card, and a rejection are distinguishable. If the response is lost, the client checks the balance and card state against the server. The claim record and balance increase are committed together.
Connection loss and account changes

Chat shows the connection loss and keeps the draft. On reconnect, it loads anything that arrived during the outage. For a send or claim with no response, the client checks the result or retries with the original operation ID.

An expired session cannot send a message or claim energy. After signing in with a different account, the previous player’s history, drafts, and events stay hidden. The current account receives updates through one subscription.
Text display and moderation
Chat renders another player’s name and message as plain text, including angle brackets. If the server rejects a message, the sender sees the reason and the recipient does not see the message.
Confirm the moderation rules, message rate limit, and how very long words wrap. To verify a rejection, check the sender’s screen, the recipient’s feed, and the server response if it is available.
Small screens and keyboard controls

With the on-screen keyboard open, the player can still send a message, switch tabs, and close chat. On a small screen and with enlarged text, controls do not overlap and the name and timestamp stay with their message.
If the game supports a keyboard and a screen reader, Tab follows a predictable order. Focus is visible and each icon is announced by its purpose.
questions: How do players open chat and a private tab?
What do the map pin, heart, shield, and icon next to the input open? How many private tabs can a player open, and can they still interact with the game outside the chat window?
Who can see channels and private messages?
Is the Café shared by the whole game, one server, or one location? What happens to history if a player leaves a channel or the other player blocks them?
When does the red dot clear?
Does opening the tab count, or does the player have to see the last message? If they read it on their phone, does the dot clear on their other device?
Who is counted as online?
Which players make up the 237? When does the count refresh, how long does a disconnected player count as online, and what does the counter show when offline?
How is chat history stored?
How long are older messages kept and how many load at a time? Which time zone and format should the date and time use?
What can players type and send?

What is the length limit and how are multi-code-point emoji counted? How should long words wrap? Are line breaks and surrounding spaces kept? When should Enter send a message, including during IME input?
What happens when the server does not respond?
When should an error appear, and how long can a retry reuse the original send operation? Can players queue a message while offline?
How do players send a sticker?
Does selecting a sticker send it right away, or does the player have to confirm? Are there paid packs? What appears if the picker is empty or fails to load?
Who can claim energy and how? · P0
How does a player create a request? Can the requester click “Claim” on their own card? Where does the energy come from, and how many players can claim from one request?
When does a request stop being usable? · P0
Is there an expiry, a daily limit, a balance cap, or a limit on recipients? If there is room for fewer than 50 units, does the player get the remainder or is the claim rejected?
What appears after a player clicks “Claim”? · P0
How does the UI distinguish a pending response from rejection, expiry, and an already successful claim? Where can the player check their final balance after losing connection?
What is kept after restarting?
Does the draft survive quitting the game? Can one account sign in on two devices? How quickly does chat catch up after reconnecting?
How does moderation work?
How many messages can be sent within one rate-limit window? What is shown when a message is rejected, and can players report or block someone from chat?
What should the UI be tested on?
Which devices, minimum window sizes, input methods, and scaling settings does the game support?
cases: CHAT-01
Open, close, and reopen chat
A is in the game and has never opened chat.
Open chat.
Use the window’s close button, then open chat again.
The first visit shows the Café feed and message field. The close button hides the window. Reopening shows the same channel without duplicating messages.
CHAT-02
Close a private tab and reopen the conversation
A has open conversations with B and C. The conversation with B already contains message m1.
Open the conversation with B and click the close button on that tab.
Reopen the conversation with B.
Chat stays open and switches to the Café. C’s tab remains open. When A reopens the conversation with B, m1 appears once.
CHAT-03
Send drafts from two different tabs
A has the Café and a private conversation with B open. B and C can both read the Café.
Type “for B only” in the private tab and “for everyone in the Café” in the public channel. Switch tabs and check the draft in each one.
Send the message from each tab. Check B’s and C’s feeds.
Each tab kept its own draft. B sees “for B only” in the private chat and “for everyone in the Café” in the public channel. C sees only the public message.
CHAT-04
Check that an outside player cannot see a private chat
A and B have a private conversation containing m1. C is signed in under a separate account. The test environment supports separate read and send checks.
Ask A to message B. Check C’s conversations and incoming events.
Using C’s session, check how the server handles attempts to read A and B’s conversation history and send a message to it.
C sees none of the conversation, its history, or A’s new message. The server rejects both operations from C. No message from C appears in A and B’s conversation.
CHAT-05
Switch tabs while history is loading
A has access to two channels with different message histories. The test environment can delay responses.
Open the first channel and hold its history response.
Open the second channel. Once its messages are visible, release the delayed response.
Send a message from the second channel.
The second tab stays active. Messages from the first channel do not appear in it. The new message reaches the second channel.
CHAT-06
Revoke channel access while the player is reading it
A is reading a restricted channel and has a draft in the message field. B will retain access.
Remove A from the channel and check whether A can send the draft.
Close and reopen chat. As B, check whether A’s text appeared.
The restricted feed disappears for A. The draft is not posted. Reopening chat takes A to a channel they can access.
CHAT-07
Show an unread message in another tab
A is reading the Café. The private tab with B is open in the background and has no unread messages.
Send a new message from B to A.
Check the red dot. Open B’s tab and scroll to the new message.
The dot appears on B’s tab. The Café stays active until A switches tabs. The dot clears once the message is in view.
CHAT-08
Receive messages while chat is closed
A has open conversations with B and C and has read both. The conversation with C is active.
Close the chat window. Send two messages from B to A.
Open chat, check the tabs, and scroll to B’s latest message.
Chat opens on C’s tab. C’s tab has no dot. B’s dot remains until A sees B’s last message.
CHAT-09
Count a player with two sessions only once
The number of players in the test channel is known. B can sign in on two devices.
Connect B’s first session, then the second. Check the count after each sign-in.
Disconnect the sessions one at a time. Allow for the agreed update delay.
Disconnect A, then reconnect.

B’s first session adds one, and the second leaves the count unchanged. The count returns to its starting value after B leaves the last device. While offline, A sees a stale count. It refreshes after reconnecting.
CHAT-10
Load earlier messages without jumping the feed
The history has at least three pages. Two adjacent responses share one ID. Message m10 is visible near the top of the feed.
Note where m10 is on screen. Load earlier messages.
Repeat at the next page boundary and scroll to the beginning of the history.
After the first load, m10 stays in place. The shared message is shown once and the order is preserved. Chat stops requesting empty pages at the beginning of the history.
CHAT-11
Deliver events out of order and more than once
The server orders the messages m1, m2, m3. The test environment can change their delivery order.
Deliver m1, then m3, then m2 twice.
Wait for sync and reopen the tab.
The feed contains three messages in the order m1, m2, m3. Reopening the tab preserves the count and order.
CHAT-12
Receive a new message while reading history
A has scrolled up in the conversation with B to read older messages.
Send a new message from B and check the position of A’s feed.
Jump to the latest messages and ask B to send another message.
The first message does not move the part A was reading. Jumping to the latest messages brings it into view. With A already at the bottom, the next message appears immediately.
CHAT-13
Check message authors and timestamps around midnight
A has a configured time zone. Two players sent messages before and after midnight in that zone.
Compare each message’s author, icon, and timestamp with the test data.
Change the time zone and refresh the feed.
Dates and times reflect the selected zone and agreed format. The names and icons are assigned to the right messages. The server order is unchanged.
CHAT-14
Send a text message to the Café
A and B are in the Café. C is in another channel. The connection is stable.
As A, use the arrow to send “Hi, Café! 🙂”.
Compare the feeds for A, B, and C. Reopen chat as A.
A sees one confirmed message and an empty input field. B sees one copy with A’s name. C does not see it. Reopening chat does not add another copy for A.
CHAT-15
Try to send an empty message
A has opened the Café. B can see the channel. The test environment can show whether a send request was issued.
Test an empty field, spaces only, tabs only, and line breaks only.
In each case, click the arrow if it is available and check whether a send request was issued.
The send action is disabled or the field shows a validation error. No request is issued and neither feed contains a blank message.
CHAT-16
Check the length limit with Cyrillic text and emoji
The limit L and the counting method are known. Test strings of length L−1, L, and L+1 include Cyrillic and multi-code-point emoji.
Try to enter and send each string.
Compare client behavior with a separate check of server validation.
The L−1 and L strings are sent in full. L+1 does not create a message. The client and server count the length the same way.
CHAT-17
Retry sending a message that already arrived
A and B are in one channel. The test environment records the message but withholds the response until the client times out.
Send “duplicate check”. Verify that B received it.
After the timeout, click Retry. Reopen the feed for A and B.
A’s original message becomes confirmed. B still sees one copy. The server ties the retry to the original send and stores one message ID.
CHAT-18
Edit a message rejected by moderation
A test phrase is blocked in the test environment. B is reading the channel.
Send the blocked phrase and check the error.
Edit the text and send it again.
A sees the reason for rejection and can edit the text. B never sees the blocked phrase. The corrected message appears once for B.
CHAT-19
Send a message over the rate limit
The limit is N messages per interval T. A has not sent anything in the current interval.
Send N valid messages and immediately try one more.
Wait for the limit to reset and send another message.
B receives the first N messages. The extra message does not appear and A sees a warning. The next send succeeds once the limit resets.
CHAT-20
Display angle brackets as plain text
A and B are in a test channel. The text “QA & ‘test’” is allowed by moderation.
Send the string from A and open it as B.
Refresh B’s history and compare the text again.
B sees the original characters, including angle brackets. The tags do not make QA bold. Neighboring messages and controls look and work as before.
CHAT-21
Send a sticker and keep the text draft
A has typed a draft in B’s private tab. A sticker is available. C is reading the public chat.
Open and close the picker without selecting a sticker.
Reopen the picker and select an available sticker.
Closing the picker sends nothing. Selecting the sticker adds one copy to each of A’s and B’s private feeds. C does not see it. A’s draft is still in the field.
CHAT-22
Check sticker rejection and an image load failure
The test environment can revoke access to one sticker and separately break image loading for a second sticker.
After opening the picker, revoke access to the first sticker and try to send it.
Send the second sticker. Check the load failure as B, restore the image, and retry loading.
The first sticker does not reach B and A sees a rejection. B sees a placeholder for the second sticker without a scroll jump. After retrying, the image appears in the same message.
CHAT-23
Claim 50 energy
A can claim energy from card r1. A’s balance is 120, the cap is at least 170, and no other balance changes are expected.
Click “Claim 50”. Check the card and balance against the test environment.
Close and reopen chat.
After the pending state, the card shows a successful claim. The balance is 170. There is one +50 entry for A and r1. The button cannot be used after reopening chat.
CHAT-24
Click Claim several times in quick succession
A has access to card r1 and has 120 energy. The cap is at least 170. The server response is delayed.
Click the button several times quickly.
Wait for the response, reopen chat, and check the balance and credit entries.
The button is disabled while the server responds. The final balance is 170 with one credit entry. A cannot claim from r1 a second time.
CHAT-25
Claim energy from two devices at once
A is signed in to the same account on two devices. Card r1 appears on both. The balance is 120 and the cap is at least 170.
Click “Claim” on both devices before the first response arrives.
Wait for both screens to update. Check the balance and credit history.
The final balance is 170 with one +50 entry. Both devices show that the energy from r1 has already been claimed.
CHAT-26
Lose the connection after energy is credited
A can claim r1 and has 120 energy. The cap is at least 170. The test environment can interrupt the connection after recording the credit.
Click “Claim 50” and cut the connection after the credit is recorded but before the response reaches the client.
Reconnect. If chat offers a retry, use it. Check r1 and the balance.
While the result is unknown, chat does not show a false success or final rejection. After checking with the server, r1 is shown as claimed. The balance is 170 with one +50 entry.
CHAT-27
Click Claim after the request expires
Card r1 has an expiry. A can see it and has a balance of 120. The test environment can advance the server clock.
Advance the server clock past r1’s expiry.
Try to claim from the screen before it refreshes, then refresh chat.
The server rejects the expired claim. The balance remains 120 and no +50 entry is created. After refreshing, the card is marked expired or hidden, according to the agreed rule.
CHAT-28
Check who can claim energy
One test player cannot see r1. A second can see it but cannot claim. Add a separate check for the requester once Q09 is answered.
As each player, check whether the card and button appear.
Use the test environment to check that the server rejects a claim from each session.
The first player does not see the card. The second has no enabled claim button. The server makes no balance changes or credit entries for either player.
CHAT-29
Claim energy near the balance cap
The balance cap C is known. The card grants 50 energy. This case assumes no partial grants until Q10 is resolved.
Set the balance to C−50, C−49, and C in separate runs. Open a new card each time and click “Claim”.
Check the balance, card state, and credit history.
Starting at C−50 brings the balance to C with one +50 entry. Starting at C−49 or C leaves the balance unchanged with no credit. The card is not marked as claimed, and the player sees the reason.
CHAT-30
Two players try to claim the last available grant
This case applies if a request has a shared recipient limit. One claim remains on r1. A and B are both eligible.
Click “Claim” as A and B at the same time.
Check the responses, both balances, and the number of claims remaining.
One player receives +50. The other is told that no claims are left and their balance is unchanged. The remaining count is zero and there is one credit entry.
CHAT-31
Catch up on messages received while offline
A is reading the Café and has typed “later” in the message field. B and C are also in the Café.
Disconnect A. Send one message each from B and C.
Reconnect A. Once synced, compare A’s feed with B’s. Switch to another tab and back.
During the outage, the connection status is visible and the draft stays in the field. Both messages appear for A in the original order without duplicates. The draft still reads “later”.
CHAT-32
Switch accounts after the first session ends
A has a private conversation with B and a draft. C can sign in on the same device. The test environment can end A’s session.
End A’s session on the server and try to send from the old window.
Sign in as C and open chat. Ask B to send a new message to A.
A’s send is rejected and does not appear for B. C sees none of A’s tabs, history, or draft. The new message from B to A is also hidden from C.
CHAT-33
Use chat with the on-screen keyboard open
Text is enlarged on the smallest supported screen. A game object sits under the chat input.
Open chat and bring up the keyboard, then send a message.
Open and close the sticker picker, switch tabs, and close chat.
The input, send arrow, tabs, and close button are reachable. Text and controls are not clipped. Clicking inside chat does not activate the object underneath.
CHAT-34
Use chat with a keyboard and screen reader
The client supports keyboard input and a screen reader. Chat has a private tab and a card available to claim.
Move through the controls using Tab and Shift+Tab.
Use the keyboard to open and close the sticker picker, send a message, and claim energy.

Focus is visible and follows a predictable order. The screen reader announces controls by their purpose. Closing the picker returns focus to the sticker button. The screen reader announces the send and claim results.
